history.hpi: Mother reports the patient has had a worsening asthma flare over the past several hours despite using her rescue inhaler more than 10 times. She has become progressively more short of breath and is now confused and difficult to arouse. She has a history of a prior ICU admission for asthma.
pastMedical: Prior ICU admission for asthma at age 13
history.events: Mother called 911 after the patient became confused and increasingly difficult to arouse despite repeated rescue inhaler use

scene.location: Single-family home, bedroom, patient slumped in a chair, rescue inhaler on the floor nearby
scene.bystanders: Mother present, extremely distressed, providing history
visualCues: Patient slumped in a chair, minimal visible chest movement
Empty rescue inhaler on the floor
No audible wheeze despite obvious distress — silent chest
Slow to respond to mother's voice

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew finds a 16-year-old female with known severe asthma who is altered, cyanotic, and has a silent chest — minimal air movement despite obvious severe distress — after excessive rescue inhaler use without relief.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent but minimal air movement audible
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Silent chest, minimal chest rise, decreasing retractions from fatigue
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Responds to voice, slow and confused
otherFindings: No audible wheeze despite obvious severe distress — a silent chest indicates minimal air movement, not improvement
Used rescue inhaler more than 10 times today without relief
History of prior ICU admission and two prior intubations for asthma
Increasing confusion and difficulty arousing per mother
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: Barely responsive, unable to speak in words

expectedActions.shortAction: Continuous albuterol 5 mg + ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulized, repeated with unlimited frequency for ongoing distress
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Albuterol 5 mg nebulized (or 6 puffs metered dose inhaler) should be administered to all patients in respiratory distress with signs of bronchospasm. Repeat at this dose with unlimited frequency for ongoing respiratory distress. Ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulized should be given up to 3 doses in conjunction with albuterol
expectedActions.rationale: Continuous bronchodilator therapy is the foundation of severe asthma management and should not be interrupted.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Respiratory Distress (includes Bronchospasm, Pulmonary Edema)

expectedActions.shortAction: Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM (1 mg/mL) (55 kg × 0.01 mg/kg = 0.55 mg → capped at max 0.3 mg); adjunctive for impending respiratory failure
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Epinephrine (0.01 mg/kg of 1 mg/mL solution IM, maximum dose of 0.3 mg) should only be administered for impending respiratory failure as adjunctive therapy when there are no clinical signs of improvement with the above treatments
expectedActions.rationale: A silent chest with altered mental status indicates impending respiratory failure, meeting criteria for adjunctive IM epinephrine.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Respiratory Distress (includes Bronchospasm, Pulmonary Edema)

expectedActions.shortAction: Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV (55 kg × 40 mg/kg = 2200 mg → capped at max 2 g) over 10-15 minutes
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Magnesium sulfate (40 mg/kg IV, maximum dose of 2 g) over 10-15 minutes should be administered for severe bronchoconstriction and concern for impending respiratory failure
expectedActions.rationale: Magnesium sulfate provides additional bronchodilation for severe bronchoconstriction unresponsive to first-line therapy.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Respiratory Distress (includes Bronchospasm, Pulmonary Edema)

transitions.if: IM epi and mag sulfate given
transitions.condition: Crew recognizes impending respiratory failure from near-fatal asthma and escalates immediately to IM epinephrine, IV magnesium sulfate, and continuous nebulized bronchodilators.

transitions.if: Escalation delayed, respiratory failure requiring RSI
transitions.condition: Crew continues standard nebulizer treatment alone without escalating to IM epinephrine or magnesium sulfate, and the patient progresses to frank respiratory failure and arrest requiring RSI.

phases.name: IM epi and mag sulfate given
phases.description: Crew recognizes the silent chest and altered mental status as signs of impending respiratory failure and escalates immediately: continuous nebulized albuterol/ipratropium, IM epinephrine as adjunctive therapy, and IV magnesium sulfate over 10-15 minutes.
phases.triggerCondition: A silent chest with altered mental status and no improvement with inhaled therapy alone meets criteria for adjunctive IM epinephrine and magnesium sulfate per protocol.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, air movement beginning to return
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Faint wheeze now audible — improving from silent chest
otherFindings: IM epinephrine given as adjunctive therapy
IV magnesium sulfate infusing over 10-15 minutes
Audible wheeze returning — a reassuring sign after a silent chest

expectedActions.shortAction: Continue non-invasive management; avoid intubation now that air movement and mental status are improving
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Invasive airways do not improve bronchospasm. The airway should be managed in the least invasive way possible. Supraglottic devices and endotracheal intubation should be considered only if BVM ventilation fails
expectedActions.rationale: Intubation in bronchospastic patients carries risk of air trapping and barotrauma and should be reserved for true respiratory failure.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Respiratory Distress (includes Bronchospasm, Pulmonary Edema)

transitions.condition: With continuous bronchodilators, IM epinephrine, and magnesium sulfate, air movement and mental status improve, avoiding the need for intubation.

phases.name: Improved, intubation avoided
phases.description: Air movement and mental status continue to improve with aggressive medical therapy. Crew avoids invasive airway management, consistent with the principle that intubation does not improve bronchospasm and should be reserved for true respiratory failure.
phases.triggerCondition: Following IM epinephrine, magnesium sulfate, and continuous bronchodilators, air movement is clearly improving and mental status is returning to baseline, avoiding the need for RSI.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, audible wheeze with improving air movement
otherFindings: Audible wheeze throughout, no longer silent
Tolerating continued nebulizer therapy en route
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I can breathe a little better now."

phases.name: Escalation delayed, respiratory failure requiring RSI
phases.description: Crew continues standard nebulizer treatment without escalating to IM epinephrine or magnesium sulfate. The patient progresses to frank respiratory failure with loss of respiratory effort, requiring RSI.
phases.triggerCondition: Without adjunctive IM epinephrine and magnesium sulfate, the silent chest and altered mental status progress to complete respiratory failure, now requiring advanced airway management.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Minimal air movement, patient no longer maintaining effective respirations
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses weak, bradycardic — an ominous sign of impending arrest
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: No purposeful movement, decorticate posturing to pain
otherFindings: No wheeze audible — complete silent chest
Bradycardia developing, a pre-arrest sign in this context

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize true respiratory failure; perform RSI with ketamine (bronchodilator properties) for induction
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Endotracheal intubation... Other indications may include potential airway obstruction. Administer induction sedative agent: Ketamine IV push, 1-2 mg/kg
expectedActions.rationale: Once true respiratory failure develops, invasive airway management is now indicated; ketamine is preferred in bronchospastic patients for its bronchodilator effect.
